units.title: Topic 1: Atomic Structure and the Periodic Table

topics.title: Atomic structure and the Periodic Table

outcomes.text: Describe an atom in terms of electrons, protons and neutrons.
State the relative mass and relative charge of each sub-atomic particle.
Explain atomic (proton) number and mass number.
Work out the numbers of each particle in an atom, molecule or ion.
Explain what isotopes are.
Define relative isotopic mass and relative atomic mass on the carbon-12 scale.
Calculate relative molecular and formula masses from relative atomic masses.
Use mass spectrometry data to find relative atomic mass from isotope abundances, and the reverse.
Predict mass spectra with peak heights for diatomic molecules such as chlorine.
Explain how the molecular ion peak gives the relative molecular mass.
Define first and successive ionisation energies.
Explain how nuclear charge, shielding and sub-shell affect ionisation energies.
Explain why first ionisation energy generally rises across a period.
Explain why first ionisation energy falls down a group.
Explain how emission spectra and ionisation energies gave evidence for shells and sub-shells.
State how many electrons fill the first four quantum shells.
Describe an orbital as holding up to two electrons of opposite spin.
Describe the shapes of s and p orbitals.
State how many electrons s, p and d sub-shells hold.
Apply the rule that electrons fill sub-shells singly before pairing.
Write electronic configurations of atoms and s/p-block ions up to Z = 36, in 1s notation and boxes.
Classify elements as s, p or d block.
Explain that electronic configuration determines chemical properties.
Describe periodicity as a repeating pattern across periods.
Explain trends in melting point, boiling point and ionisation energy across periods 2 and 3.
Illustrate periodicity with data on configurations, radii, melting points and ionisation energies.
State that ionic bonding is strong attraction between oppositely charged ions.
Explain how ionic radius and charge affect ionic bond strength.
Describe ion formation by electron loss or gain.
Draw dot-and-cross diagrams of cations and anions.
Explain trends in ionic radii down a group and across isoelectronic ions.
Explain how ionic compounds' properties and ion migration show that ions exist.
State that a covalent bond is attraction between two nuclei and a shared electron pair.
Draw dot-and-cross diagrams for single, double, triple and dative covalent bonds, including Al2Cl6 and ammonium.
Relate bond length to bond strength.
Explain that molecular shape comes from repulsion between electron pairs round a central atom.
Explain shapes and bond angles for species with up to six outer pairs, such as BeCl2, CH4, NH3, H2O, PCl5, SF6.
Predict shapes and bond angles of similar molecules and ions.
Define electronegativity.
Explain ionic and covalent bonding as a continuum, with bond polarity from electronegativity differences.
Predict whether a molecule with polar bonds is polar overall.
Describe London forces, permanent dipoles and hydrogen bonds.
Identify the interactions giving hydrogen bonding in H2O, NH3 and HF.
Explain water's high melting and boiling points and the density of ice.
Predict hydrogen bonding in similar molecules.
Explain boiling point trends of alkanes, branched alkanes, alcohols and hydrogen halides using intermolecular forces.
Explain solvent choice: water for ionic compounds and alcohols, poor for halogenoalkanes, and non-aqueous solvents with matching forces.
State that metallic bonding is attraction between metal ions and delocalised electrons.
Identify giant ionic, giant covalent and giant metallic lattices.
State that substances such as iodine and ice are simple molecular.
Describe the structures of graphite, diamond and graphene.
Predict structure and bonding type from data.
Predict melting point, conductivity and solubility from particles, structure and bonding.
Define oxidation number.
Calculate oxidation numbers in compounds and ions, including peroxides and metal hydrides.
Write oxidation numbers using Roman numerals.
Write formulae from given oxidation numbers.
Describe oxidation and reduction as electron transfer and oxidation number change in s- and p-block reactions.
Describe oxidation as electron loss and reduction as electron gain.
State that oxidising agents gain electrons.
State that reducing agents lose electrons.
Explain that metals form positive ions with increased oxidation number.
Explain that non-metals form negative ions with decreased oxidation number.
Explain disproportionation as one element in one species being oxidised and reduced at once.
Use oxidation numbers to classify reactions as redox or disproportionation.
Write ionic half-equations and combine them into full ionic equations.

units.title: Topic 4: Inorganic Chemistry and the Periodic Table

topics.title: Topic 4A: The elements of Groups 1 and 2

outcomes.text: Explain the trend in ionisation energy down Group 2.
Explain the trend in reactivity down Group 2.
Recall reactions of Mg to Ba with oxygen, chlorine and water.
Recall reactions of Group 2 oxides with water and acid, and hydroxides with acid.
State trends in solubility of Group 2 hydroxides and sulfates.
Explain trends in thermal stability of Group 1 and 2 nitrates and carbonates using cation size and charge.
Explain flame colours of Group 1 and 2 compounds by electron transitions, and recall the colours.
Describe experiments on thermal decomposition and flame colours.
Explain trends in melting point, boiling point, state and electronegativity in Group 7.
Explain the trend in halogen reactivity down the group.
Explain halogen reactivity using redox reactions of Cl2, Br2 and I2 with halide ions.
Explain halogen reactions with metals, water, cold dilute alkali and hot alkali using oxidation number changes.
Explain reactions of halides with concentrated sulfuric acid, silver nitrate then ammonia, and hydrogen halides with ammonia and water.
Predict properties of fluorine, astatine and their compounds from trends.
Recall tests for carbonate and hydrogencarbonate, sulfate and ammonium ions with ionic equations.

units.title: Topic 5: Formulae, Equations and Amounts of Substance

topics.title: Formulae, equations and amounts of substance

outcomes.text: State that the mole is the unit of amount of substance.
Use the Avogadro constant in calculations.
Define molar mass in g per mol.
Distinguish empirical and molecular formulae.
Calculate empirical and molecular formulae from data, using pV = nRT for gases and volatile liquids.
Write balanced full and ionic equations with state symbols.
Calculate amounts in moles from mass, gas volume, solution volume and concentration.
Calculate reacting masses from equations and the reverse.
Calculate reacting gas volumes using amount of substance.
Calculate reacting gas volumes using molar volume. Core practical 1: measure the molar volume of a gas.
Calculate concentrations in mol per dm3 and g per dm3, including acid-base titrations with phenolphthalein and methyl orange. Core practicals 2 and 3: standard solution and titration.
Calculate measurement uncertainties and errors and comment on error sources.
Explain how to minimise percentage error and uncertainty.
Calculate percentage yield and percentage atom economy.
Relate ionic and full equations to observations in displacement, acid and precipitation reactions.
Explain risks and hazards in practical work and suggest precautions.
Define a hydrocarbon as a compound of hydrogen and carbon only.
Represent organic molecules with empirical, molecular, general, structural, displayed and skeletal formulae.
Define homologous series and functional group.
Name compounds using IUPAC rules, with prefixes up to C10.
Classify reactions as addition, elimination, substitution, oxidation, reduction, hydrolysis or polymerisation.
Explain structural isomerism and draw the possible isomers of a molecular formula.
Explain stereoisomerism through E/Z isomerism, including cis-trans.
State the general formula of alkanes.
State that alkanes and cycloalkanes are saturated.
Explain that fuels come from fractional distillation, cracking and reforming of crude oil.
Name pollutants from burning alkanes: CO, oxides of nitrogen and sulfur, particulates, unburned hydrocarbons.
Explain the problems from toxic CO and acidic nitrogen and sulfur oxides.
Explain how a catalytic converter reduces pollutants.
Compare alternative fuels such as biodiesel and bioalcohols with fossil fuels.
Define a radical and homolytic fission.
Explain alkane combustion and the radical substitution mechanism with halogens: initiation, propagation, termination.
Explain the limits of radical substitution in synthesis: further substitution and mixtures.
State the general formula of alkenes.
State that alkenes and cycloalkenes are unsaturated.
Describe the sigma and pi bonding in alkenes.
Define an electrophile.
Explain addition of hydrogen, halogens, hydrogen halides, steam and acidified manganate(VII) to alkenes.
Explain that heterolytic fission gives ions.
Describe electrophilic addition of halogens and hydrogen halides, including unsymmetrical alkenes and carbocation stability, with curly arrows.
Recall the bromine water test for a C=C bond.
Explain addition polymerisation and identify repeat units and monomers.
Describe how waste polymers are recycled, incinerated or used as cracking feedstock.
Explain how life-cycle energy and resource use shows chemists' contribution to sustainability.
Describe biodegradable polymers and removing toxic gases from incineration.
Classify halogenoalkanes as primary, secondary or tertiary.
Define a nucleophile.
Explain reactions of halogenoalkanes with aqueous KOH, aqueous silver nitrate, KCN, ammonia and ethanolic KOH.
Compare hydrolysis rates of primary, secondary, tertiary and chloro-, bromo-, iodo-alkanes using silver nitrate. Core practical 4.
State the reactivity trend of primary, secondary and tertiary halogenoalkanes.
Explain the reactivity trend of C-Cl, C-Br and C-I using bond enthalpy.
Describe nucleophilic substitution mechanisms of primary halogenoalkanes with hydroxide and ammonia.
Classify alcohols as primary, secondary or tertiary.
Explain alcohol combustion, halogenation, oxidation with dichromate and dehydration to alkenes.
Explain heating under reflux, solvent extraction, distillation, drying and boiling point determination. Core practicals 5 and 6.
Use mass spectra to find relative molecular mass from the molecular ion and suggest structures from fragmentation.
Use infrared spectra to identify functional groups and predict absorptions for C-H, C=C, O-H, C=O and N-H stretches. Core practical 7: analyse unknowns.
State standard conditions as 100 kPa and usually 298 K.
Define enthalpy change as heat change at constant pressure.
Construct and interpret enthalpy level diagrams with correct signs.
Define standard enthalpy changes of reaction, formation, combustion and neutralisation.
Process calorimetry results with Q = mc delta T and evaluate errors and assumptions.
Calculate enthalpy changes in kJ per mol from experimental results, with sign and units.
Construct enthalpy cycles using Hess's law.
Calculate enthalpy changes from data using Hess's law. Core practical 8.
Define bond enthalpy and mean bond enthalpy.
Calculate reaction enthalpy from mean bond enthalpies and explain the method's limits.
Calculate mean bond enthalpies from reaction enthalpies.
Explain with collision theory how concentration, temperature, pressure and surface area change rate.
State that reactions need collisions with at least the activation energy.
Calculate rate from reaction time or from a graph's tangent gradient.
Explain qualitatively how temperature affects rate using the Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution.
Explain catalysts as providing a lower-activation-energy route.
Draw reaction profiles for uncatalysed and catalysed reactions.
Interpret catalyst action using the Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution.
Explain solid heterogeneous catalysts in gas-phase industrial reactions as providing a surface.
Explain the economic benefits of industrial catalysts.
Describe dynamic equilibrium: forward and backward rates equal and concentrations constant.
Predict and justify the effect of changing temperature, concentration or pressure on equilibrium.
Evaluate data showing the compromise between yield and rate in industrial processes.
Deduce Kc expressions for homogeneous and heterogeneous systems.
Deduce Kp expressions from partial pressures in atm.
Calculate Kc and Kp with units from experimental data.
State how temperature changes Kc and Kp for exothermic and endothermic reactions.
Explain the temperature effect on equilibrium position through the constant's value.
State that concentration, pressure and catalysts do not change the equilibrium constant.
Define Brønsted-Lowry acids as proton donors and bases as proton acceptors.
State that acid-base reactions transfer protons.
Identify conjugate acid-base pairs.
Define pH.
Calculate pH from hydrogen ion concentration.
Calculate hydrogen ion concentration from pH using 10 to the minus pH.
Distinguish strong and weak acids by degree of dissociation.
Calculate the pH of a strong acid.
Deduce the Ka expression for a weak acid and do calculations.
Calculate the pH of a weak acid with sensible assumptions.
Define pKa and pKw.
Calculate Ka from the pH of a solution of known acid mass.
Define the ionic product of water, Kw.
Calculate the pH of a strong base using Kw.
Analyse data on pH of acids, bases and salts and on diluting strong and weak acids.
Draw and interpret titration curves for strong and weak monobasic acid and base combinations.
Choose a suitable indicator from a titration curve.
Define a buffer solution.
Explain how a buffer works.
Calculate the pH of a buffer.
Calculate concentrations needed to prepare a buffer of given pH.
Use a weak acid-strong base curve to show buffering and find Ka at half-neutralisation.
Explain the different neutralisation enthalpies of strong and weak acids.
Explain how carbonic acid and hydrogencarbonate control blood pH. Core practical 9: finding Ka.
Define lattice energy as the energy change forming one mole of ionic solid from gaseous ions.
Define enthalpy of atomisation and electron affinity.
Construct Born-Haber cycles and do calculations.
State that lattice energy measures ionic bond strength.
Explain that experimental versus theoretical lattice energy shows covalent character.
Explain ion polarisation.
State that a cation's polarising power depends on radius and charge.
State that an anion's polarisability depends on radius and charge.
Define enthalpy of solution and of hydration.
Use energy cycles to calculate with solution, hydration and lattice enthalpies.
Explain how ionic charge and radius affect lattice energy and hydration enthalpy.
Explain why enthalpy alone cannot decide whether reactions happen.
Define entropy as disorder and state that total entropy increases naturally.
Explain entropy changes in state changes, dissolving and mole-number changes.
State that total entropy change is system plus surroundings.
Calculate system entropy change from given entropies.
Calculate surroundings entropy change as minus delta H over T, and total entropy change.
Explain that the entropy-enthalpy balance gives feasibility via delta G = delta H minus T delta S.
Use delta G to predict feasibility and the temperature of feasibility.
Use delta G = minus RT ln K to link feasibility to large K.
Explain why a negative delta G reaction may not happen in practice.
State that feasible reactions can be kinetically inhibited.
Describe oxidation and reduction as electron transfer for s-, p- and d-block elements.
Describe them as oxidation number changes for s-, p- and d-block elements.
Define standard electrode potential.
State the standard conditions: 298 K, 100 kPa, 1.00 mol per dm3.
Describe the standard hydrogen electrode and why a reference is needed.
Explain methods of measuring potentials of metals/non-metals and of ions with different oxidation numbers. Core practical 10.
Calculate standard cell emf by combining electrode potentials.
Write cell diagrams in conventional notation.
Explain the importance of conditions when measuring electrode potential.
Predict thermodynamic feasibility using standard electrode potentials.
Explain that cell emf is proportional to total entropy change and to ln K.
Explain limits of predictions: kinetic inhibition and non-standard conditions.
Describe the electrochemical series.
Relate disproportionation to electrode potentials.
Explain electrode potentials in storage cells.
Explain how fuel cells turn fuel and oxygen energy into voltage, including methanol and hydrogen-rich fuels.
Recall electrode reactions in hydrogen-oxygen fuel cells with acid and alkaline electrolytes.
Do titration calculations including Fe2+/MnO4- and I2/S2O3 2-.
Explain methods of redox titrations. Core practical 11.

topics.title: Topic 15A: Principles of transition metal chemistry

outcomes.text: Deduce configurations of period 4 d-block atoms and ions.
Define transition metals as forming stable ions with incomplete d-orbitals.
Explain variable oxidation number.
Define a ligand.
Explain dative bonding in complex ions.
Define a complex ion as a central metal ion surrounded by ligands.
Define coordination number.
Explain why H2O, OH- and NH3 are monodentate.
Explain why six-coordinate complexes are octahedral.
State that transition metals form coloured ions in solution.
Explain colour as d-orbital splitting by ligands.
Explain why some ions are colourless.
Explain colour changes from oxidation number, ligand or coordination number changes.
State that large ligands such as Cl- give tetrahedral complexes.
State that square planar complexes form, as in cis-platin.
Explain why cis-platin is supplied as a single isomer.
Identify bidentate and multidentate ligands such as EDTA.
State that haemoglobin is an iron(II) complex with a multidentate ligand.
Describe ligand exchange when carbon monoxide replaces oxygen in haemoglobin.

topics.title: Topic 15B: Reactions of transition metal elements

outcomes.text: Recall the colours of vanadium oxidation states +5 to +2.
Explain vanadium interconversions using Eo values.
Explain, with Eo values, dichromate(VI) reduction to Cr3+ and Cr2+ and formation from Cr3+.
Describe the dichromate-chromate equilibrium.
Record observations and write equations for Cr3+, Fe2+, Fe3+, Co2+ and Cu2+ with sodium hydroxide and ammonia.
Write ionic equations distinguishing ligand exchange from amphoteric behaviour.
Explain ligand exchange colour changes for copper and cobalt complexes.
Explain how larger charged ligands can change coordination number.
Explain the extra stability of complexes with bidentate or multidentate ligands through entropy.
State that transition metals act as heterogeneous and homogeneous catalysts.
Define a heterogeneous catalyst and describe surface reaction.
Explain V2O5 catalysis in the contact process by oxidation numbers.
Explain a catalytic converter: adsorption, bond weakening and desorption.
Define a homogeneous catalyst with an intermediate species.
Explain Fe2+ catalysis of the iodide-peroxodisulfate reaction.
Explain autocatalysis by Mn2+ in the manganate-ethanedioate reaction. Core practical 12.
Define rate, rate equation, order, overall order, rate constant, half-life, rate-determining step, activation energy and catalyst types.
Determine and use rate equations of the form rate = k[A]m[B]n.
Select and justify techniques such as titration, colorimetry, mass change and gas volume.
Explain initial-rate and continuous-monitoring methods.
Calculate rate and half-life of first-order reactions from graphs.
Deduce order from concentration-time and rate-concentration graphs.
Deduce order from initial-rate data.
Explain the iodination of propanone experiment and mechanism deduction.
Deduce rate-determining step from rate equation and vice versa.
Deduce a mechanism from a rate equation and stoichiometry.
Explain how rate equations give evidence for SN1 and SN2 hydrolysis mechanisms.
Find activation energy graphically from experimental data. Core practicals 13a, 13b and 14.
Explain optical isomerism as chirality with a single chiral centre.
Explain chiral centres as asymmetric carbons giving non-superimposable mirror images.
Define optical activity as rotating plane-polarised light.
Describe a racemic mixture.
Use optical activity data as evidence for SN1 and SN2.
Identify aldehyde and ketone functional groups.
Explain how absence of hydrogen bonding between molecules and hydrogen bonding with water affect properties.
Explain carbonyl reactions with Fehling's, Tollens', dichromate, LiAlH4, HCN/KCN, 2,4-DNPH and iodine in alkali.
Identify the carboxylic acid group.
Explain how hydrogen bonding affects carboxylic acids' boiling point and solubility.
Explain preparing carboxylic acids by oxidation or nitrile hydrolysis.
Explain acid reactions with LiAlH4, bases, PCl5 and alcohols.
Identify acyl chloride and ester groups.
Explain acyl chloride reactions with water, alcohols, ammonia and amines.
Explain ester hydrolysis in acid and alkali.
Explain polyester formation by condensation polymerisation.
Describe the Kekulé and delocalised models of benzene bonding.
Explain evidence for delocalisation from hydrogenation enthalpies and bond lengths.
Explain why benzene resists bromination compared with alkenes.
Explain benzene's reactions: combustion, bromination, nitration and Friedel-Crafts.
Explain electrophilic substitution mechanisms and electrophile generation.
Explain phenol's reaction with bromine water.
Explain why phenol brominates more easily than benzene.

topics.title: Topic 18B: Amines, amides, amino acids and proteins

outcomes.text: Identify amine and amide groups and amino acids.
Explain primary aliphatic amine reactions with water, acids, ethanoyl chloride, halogenoalkanes and copper(II).
Explain differences in basicity of ammonia, aliphatic and aromatic amines.
Explain preparing primary amines from halogenoalkanes and by reducing nitriles.
State that aromatic nitro compounds are reduced to amines with tin and HCl.
State that amides are prepared from acyl chlorides.
State that polyamide formation is condensation polymerisation.
Draw repeat units of condensation polymers from diacids with diols or diamines, and amino acids.
Explain 2-amino-acid properties: zwitterions and effect on polarised light.
Explain peptide bond formation, hydrolysis and chromatographic separation. Core practical 15.
Deduce formulae from combustion analysis, composition, reactions, IR, mass spectra and NMR.
Plan reaction schemes of up to four steps.
Explain lengthening carbon chains with Grignard reagents.
Select and justify practical procedures with risk control based on hazard data.
Explain reflux, washing, solvent extraction, recrystallisation, drying, distillation and melting/boiling point determination. Core practical 16.
Use accurate relative molecular masses to suggest structures and identify compounds.
Explain that 13C NMR shows positions of carbon atoms.
Predict carbon environments from chemical shift and justify peak numbers.
Explain that high-resolution proton NMR shows positions of hydrogen atoms.
Interpret 1H NMR: shifts, peak areas, and (n+1) splitting, and predict spectra.
Explain chromatography as separation between mobile and stationary phases.
Calculate Rf values from one-way chromatograms.
Describe HPLC and GC as column methods using retention times, and their use with mass spectrometry.
